historical_timeline.summary: Moved to Toronto; Voluntary Aid Detachment work at the Spadina Military Hospital.
Severe sinus illness during the influenza epidemic, treated with sinus drainage.
Sinus operation for chronic sinus headaches, before returning to Columbia for the winter of 1924 to 1925.
Transatlantic flight in the Friendship, as a passenger.
First woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
Disappeared over the Pacific; radio contact lost.
Declared legally dead by the Superior Court in Los Angeles.

claims.statement: Amelia Mary Earhart was born on July 24, 1897, in Atchison, Kansas, to Amy Otis and Edwin Stanton Earhart.

After visiting her sister in Toronto at Christmas 1917, she moved there in February 1918 and worked in the Voluntary Aid Detachment at the Spadina Military Hospital, often on twelve-hour shifts, going wherever an extra pair of hands was needed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her wartime hospital work anchors the modern social history (an interest in medicine).

source_links.locator: February 1918, Voluntary Aid Detachment nurse at the Spadina Military Convalescent Hospital

claims.statement: During the 1918 influenza epidemic she worked nights on the ward that held the influenza patients; within weeks she fell ill herself, with severe sinus pain and terrible headaches. Her case was serious enough that doctors operated, opening into her sinuses so that they could be drained regularly. It was a month before she was well enough to leave hospital, and she went to recover at her sister's home in Massachusetts.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode. The account comes from a Toronto historian's article; no medical record was fetched, and which sinus was involved and how many drainage procedures she had are not stated in the fetched sources.

claims.statement: She suffered from chronic sinus problems for the rest of her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The reason the modern episode centers on chronic rhinosinusitis.

claims.statement: She entered Columbia University as a pre-medical student in the fall of 1919 and left in 1920. She took her first airplane ride in December 1920, with the pilot Frank Hawks, and became a licensed pilot in the early 1920s: Purdue University dates her pilot's license to May 1923, and the Encyclopedia of the Great Plains to 1921.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her flying anchors the modern occupational history; the modern episode makes her a private pilot.

source_links.locator: Columbia in the fall of 1919; first airplane ride in December 1920; license in May 1923

claims.statement: After undergoing a sinus operation to relieve her chronic sinus headaches, she returned to Columbia University for the winter of 1924 to 1925.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only. The modern episode's sinus surgery is synthetic and is not a claim about this operation.

claims.statement: In modern terms, sinus disease that began with a severe sinus infection during influenza, needed drainage operations, and caused lasting headaches and sinus trouble fits chronic rhinosinusitis. The fetched sources give no diagnosis in those terms, and nothing is known of her sinus anatomy or of nasal polyps.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective reading made for this record; the modern diagnosis is synthetic.

source_links.locator: sinus operation to relieve chronic sinus headaches

claims.statement: She accompanied the pilot Wilmer Stultz and the mechanic Louis Gordon on their 1928 transatlantic flight in the Friendship, but did not fly the plane herself. In May 1932 she became the first woman, and the second person, to fly solo across the Atlantic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only.

source_links.locator: May 20 and 21, 1932, solo transatlantic flight from Newfoundland to Ireland

claims.statement: In February 1931 she married the publisher George Palmer Putnam in Noank, Connecticut.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history only. No modern role is given to any real person.

claims.statement: Radio contact with her aircraft was lost on July 2, 1937, during her attempt to fly around the world; she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared over the Pacific. She was declared legally dead in 1939 by the Superior Court in Los Angeles.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, stated without speculation about her fate.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 25-year-old private pilot with chronic sinus symptoms: diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis by symptoms plus objective evidence (nasal endoscopy), the SNOT-22 symptom score, a check for conditions that change management, high-volume saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid as first-line treatment, a culture-directed antibiotic only for an acute exacerbation with pus and no oral steroid for disease without polyps, CT of the sinuses only after appropriate medical therapy, the appropriateness criteria for endoscopic sinus surgery and a shared decision about it, and aviation medicine: sinus and ear barotrauma, not flying while symptomatic, a 48-hour ground trial of new medicines, which medicines the FAA accepts for pilots, and return to flying after surgery, on the AAO-HNS adult sinusitis guideline (1912 update), the ICAR rhinosinusitis consensus (1918), the RAND/UCLA appropriateness criteria for sinus surgery, and the FAA Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Earhart returns two weeks after her first visit, on the day of her otolaryngology appointment, and is seen the same day by Dr. Lindgren. She has rinsed with saline twice daily and used fluticasone every morning since the first visit, and has not used a decongestant spray or the nighttime cold tablet. Five days ago the left side became worse again: the drainage turned thick and yellow-green, the pressure over the left cheek and forehead increased, and her left upper teeth ache. She has felt warm, and her temperature today is 37.6 °C. Her eosinophil count and total IgE from the first visit were normal. She has not flown since the first visit. SNOT-22 today 58, from 52.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Earhart is a 25-year-old private pilot who comes for her yearly preventive visit four weeks after her first visit for chronic sinus symptoms. Chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps was confirmed by nasal endoscopy two weeks ago, during a flare with pus on the left. She finished ten days of amoxicillin-clavulanate five days ago; the culture grew Haemophilus influenzae that makes beta-lactamase and is sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanate. The discolored drainage has stopped and the left cheek pressure is less, but her nose is still blocked most days and her sense of smell has not come back. She rinses with saline twice daily and uses the fluticasone spray every morning, with no nosebleeds. She has not flown since the endoscopy, and she stopped the nighttime cold tablet. Her SNOT-22 today is 44, from 52 at the first visit and 58 during the flare. Nobody from the clinic called her at the end of the antibiotic course, as had been planned; she would have called if she had been worse.

documentation.chief_complaint: Left ear pain and muffled hearing since a flight yesterday

hpi.narrative: Ms. Earhart called the clinic and was seen the same day. She flew yesterday as a passenger on an airline flight to visit her sister, on the third day of a head cold. During the descent her left ear blocked and became very painful; swallowing and yawning did not clear it. The pain has eased to an ache, but the ear feels full and sounds are muffled, and her own voice sounds loud in that ear. She has had no spinning, unsteadiness, ringing, discharge from the ear, or fever. Her right ear cleared normally. The cold has added clear drainage and a scratchy throat to her usual blockage. She has kept up the saline rinses and fluticasone, has not used any decongestant, and has not flown as a pilot since the endoscopy.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Earhart returns five and a half weeks after left endoscopic sinus surgery, done as day surgery without complications. She needed acetaminophen for about a week and no stronger painkiller. Dr. Lindgren cleaned the sinus cavities in the otolaryngology clinic at one and three weeks; at three weeks the left maxillary opening, ethmoid cavity and frontal recess were open and healing, she could clear her ears normally, and he cleared her to fly. She has since flown four times as pilot without any pressure pain on descent. Her nose is clear on most days, her smell is coming back, and she sleeps through the night. She rinses with saline and budesonide every morning and with plain saline at night. The pathology showed chronic inflammation without many eosinophils, with no fungus and no tumor. SNOT-22 today 12.

consultant_note.history: Ms. Earhart, a 25-year-old private pilot, is seen at the request of Dr. Talbot. She has had five months of nasal blockage, discolored drainage, pressure over the left cheek and forehead, and reduced smell, with pressure pain on descent when flying. Years ago a severe sinus infection during an influenza illness was treated in hospital with drainage operations; she does not know which sinuses were opened. She started saline irrigation and fluticasone two weeks ago. Five days ago the left side worsened, with thicker yellow-green drainage, more pressure, and aching left upper teeth. She has no asthma, aspirin sensitivity, or frequent infections, and has never smoked. She has not flown since the first visit
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Talbot's intake note. Eosinophils 0.21 x10^3/uL and total IgE 42 IU/mL, both normal. SNOT-22 52 at intake and 58 today; facial pain 6 of 10 at intake and 7 today. No imaging

exam.finding: Well; temperature 37.6 °C, pulse 80
Tender over the left maxillary sinus; no eyelid swelling; eye movements and vision normal

Swollen mucosa and thick mucopurulent drainage from the left middle meatus; mild edema of the right middle meatus without pus; no polyps on either side; mild septal deviation to the right, not blocking the middle meatus; nasopharynx normal. Culture taken from the left middle meatus
Both tympanic membranes normal

assessment.assessment: Her symptoms for more than 12 weeks with edema and pus in the middle meatus on endoscopy confirm chronic rhinosinusitis, as the AAO-HNS guideline requires; there are no polyps, and normal eosinophils and IgE without asthma suggest disease without type 2 inflammation. The worsening of the past five days is an acute exacerbation with pus, and a short course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, guided by the culture, is reasonable. An oral steroid is not advised, because the evidence for it is in disease with polyps. Saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid remain the basis of treatment. A CT is not needed now: there are no warning signs, and a CT is best done after about eight more weeks of medical therapy if symptoms persist, to judge whether surgery is appropriate and to plan it. Surgery is appropriate if the CT shows disease and the SNOT-22 stays at 20 or more after that therapy; it is her choice. The aching left upper teeth deserve a dental check, because a dental source can cause one-sided disease. Her old drainage operations do not change this plan; the CT will show any scarring. For flying: she must not fly while blocked or in pain, because a blocked sinus or ear cannot equalize on descent; the saline rinse and nasal steroid are acceptable for pilots; any new medicine needs a 48-hour ground trial; sedating antihistamines are no-go medicines. A decongestant does not make it safe to fly with a cold

Offer endoscopic sinus surgery if the CT shows disease and the SNOT-22 is 20 or more after appropriate medical therapy, as a shared decision
Dental check for the aching left upper teeth
No flying while blocked or in pain; a 48-hour ground trial of each new medicine; no sedating antihistamines; clear the ears and sinuses early and often on descent
Seek care at once for eye swelling, vision change, severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion
